screens.title: Objective deep-dive
screens.narratorSegment: This page unpacks how the objectives map to specific risk reductions. Using a centralized secret store prevents credentials from leaking in source control or build logs. Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Objective deep-dive

How objectives reduce risk

Each objective addresses a class of pipeline risk. Below are short rationale cards and a small mnemonic to help you remember the defensive layer each objective provides.

Secrets: confidentiality
Centralizing secrets prevents leaks to source control and enables rotation policies.
Image scanning: integrity
Catches known CVEs before images are deployed.
SAST & SCA: shift left
Detect code and dependency vulnerabilities early in the build.
DAST: runtime checks
Find issues only visible when the app runs in a realistic environment.
Mnemonic

Quick checklist

  • Grant CodeBuild only retrieval permissions needed
  • Use ECR scanning and block critical CVEs

screens.title: CI/CD pipeline security: definition and threat model
screens.narratorSegment: A CI/CD pipeline automates code movement from source control to production, and that automation makes it powerful but also a high-value target. When we talk about pipeline security, we mean protecting the secrets the pipeline needs, the build and test environments it runs in, the artifacts it produces, and the permissions the pipeline holds. A simple threat model includes credential theft from source or logs, compromised build agents that exfiltrate artifacts, unauthorized promotions to production, and supply-chain insertion of malicious code via third-party dependencies or base images. Defenses map to these threats: secrets must be centralized and rotated so credentials are never committed; build agents should be ephemeral and hardened; artifacts should be scanned for known vulnerabilities, and IAM roles must be tightened with least privilege. A common misconception is that running pipelines in private networks alone is sufficient. Network controls help, but they do not stop leaked secrets or an overprivileged role from acting. For a concrete example, consider an attacker obtaining a long-lived token embedded in a repository — that token can be used to trigger builds and push malicious images. The takeaway: treat the pipeline as code and infrastructure that requires the same security rigor as production systems. How would you prioritize these defenses for your environment?

keyIdea.text: Pipeline security protects secrets, build agents, artifacts, and permissions to prevent unauthorized changes and supply-chain compromise.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › CI/CD pipeline security
Core Concept

Pipeline as an attack surface

The pipeline has access to code, secrets, build environments, and deployment targets. Each is a potential leverage point for attackers.

Threats
  • Credential leakage in repos or logs
  • Compromised build agents or images
  • Unauthorized artifact promotion
  • Supply-chain tampering via dependencies
Defenses
  • Centralized secrets with rotation
  • Ephemeral, hardened build environments
  • Artifact scanning and gated promotion
  • Least-privilege IAM roles
Key Takeaway

Treat the pipeline as production: secure its credentials, environments, artifacts, and permissions to reduce supply-chain risk.

Analogy
Think of your pipeline as a factory assembly line. If a malicious component is introduced early, every product that follows is compromised. Controls at each station — guarded access to tools, scanning of parts, and strict operator permissions — are required to prevent defective or malicious products from reaching customers.
Secrets
Never embed credentials; retrieve them securely.
Build agents
Use ephemeral workers and hardened images.
Artifacts
Scan and gate on vulnerabilities before promotion.

screens.title: Secret Management: purpose and options
screens.narratorSegment: Secrets are sensitive values required at build or runtime: database passwords, A P I keys, and tokens. Centralized secret management prevents developers from embedding those values in code or configuration files where they can leak. AWS provides two primary services for this purpose: Secrets Manager and Systems Manager Parameter Store. Secrets Manager is designed for credentials and supports automatic rotation for services like databases. It is suited to secrets that require periodic rotation or broad auditing. Parameter Store also supports secure strings and is suitable for configuration values and non-rotating secrets; it is often used for environment-specific parameters or feature flags. The practical difference comes down to rotation features and operational patterns. A common misconception is that Parameter Store is insecure; when used with SecureString and proper KMS keys it is secure, but it lacks Secrets Manager’s built-in rotation workflow. For a concrete example, store a DB password in Secrets Manager and grant CodeBuild’s service role permission to retrieve that secret during build, rather than checking it into source. The key takeaway is to never hardcode secrets: centralize, grant narrowly, and enable rotation when possible.

keyIdea.text: Use Secrets Manager for rotating credentials and Parameter Store SecureString for configuration and non-rotating secrets, always retrieving at runtime.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Secret Management
Definition

Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store

Both store secrets securely, but Secrets Manager adds rotation and credential lifecycle features while Parameter Store is lightweight and ideal for configuration.

AWS Secrets Manager
Automatic rotation, auditing, and integrations for credentials.
SSM Parameter Store
SecureString parameters for config and simple secrets without rotation workflows.
Concrete example
Store a DB password in Secrets Manager and grant CodeBuild permission to get-secret-value. The build can then read the value as an environment variable without ever committing it.
Misconception
Some teams assume Parameter Store is less secure. When SecureString and KMS are used, Parameter Store can be secure, but it lacks Secrets Manager's rotation features and credential lifecycle automation.
Pro tip

Favor Secrets Manager for rotating database credentials; use Parameter Store for static config and feature flags.

Why it matters
Rotation and centralized access reduce long-lived secrets and make audits and revocation practical when a credential is suspected compromised.

screens.title: Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between Secrets Manager and Parameter Store depends on your operational needs. Secrets Manager is purpose-built for credentials: it supports built-in rotation with Lambda rotation functions, fine-grained resource policies, and auditing of secret retrieval. Use it when secrets require regular rotation or you need lifecycle automation. Parameter Store, with SecureString, is well suited to configuration, non-rotating secrets, and feature flags, and it can be simpler and lower cost for many parameters. A practical scenario: use Secrets Manager for your database password that should be rotated every 30 days, and use Parameter Store for an environment toggle or a service endpoint URL that rarely changes. A common mistake is mirroring all secrets into a single store without considering rotation risk — rotation workflows should be applied where credentials are used by many services. In pipelines, both services can be retrieved by CodeBuild using env-level secret references. The most important rule is to grant only the required get permissions to your builds and to avoid printing secrets in logs. A short test you can run: ensure secrets are never visible in build logs even when an error occurs.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store
AWS Secrets Manager
Automatic rotation, credential lifecycle, fine-grained policies, and auditing. Ideal for database credentials and API keys that require rotation.
When to choose
Rotating DB passwords, central credential management with rotation workflows.
Operational notes
Support for Lambda rotation functions and integrated auditing of secret usage.
SSM Parameter Store
SecureString parameters for configuration values and non-rotating secrets. Simpler billing and good for environment variables and feature toggles.
When to choose
Static config, many small parameters, or where rotation is not required.
Operational notes
Use with KMS keys for SecureString and scope GetParameter permissions for builds.
Common mistake

Treating Parameter Store as a drop-in replacement for Secrets Manager when rotation is required. Choose based on rotation and lifecycle needs.

screens.title: Integrating secrets into CodeBuild
screens.narratorSegment: This screen walks through a typical CodeBuild integration where a secret stored in Secrets Manager is made available to the build as an environment variable. The important idea is that the buildspec references the secret by ARN under the env -> secrets-manager section, and CodeBuild’s service role must be permitted to call GetSecretValue for that secret ARN. The build then uses the environment variable without printing it to logs. A common pitfall is echoing the secret during debugging; never print secrets to stdout. Here is a minimal buildspec pattern: define the secret mapping so CodeBuild resolves the value at runtime, then use it in commands. Remember to scope the service role policy to only that secret and to deny broad wildcard secrets. In practice, you would also ensure the CodeBuild project uses an ephemeral image, and that any custom image is hardened and scanned. The takeaway: runtime secret injection via Secrets Manager eliminates committed credentials, but role permissions and log hygiene must be enforced to keep it safe. Integrating secrets into CodeBuild means reference secrets by arn in buildspec.yml and grant codebuild getsecretvalue only for those arns; never echo secrets in logs.. In practical terms, using buildspec.yml to retrieve secrets manager values securely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Integrating secrets into CodeBuild
Code Walkthrough

Example buildspec.yml secret injection

version: 0.2
env:
  secrets-manager:
    DB_PASSWORD: "arn:aws:secretsmanager:REGION:ACCOUNT_ID:secret:my-db-secret-xxxxxx"
phases:
  build:
    commands:
      - echo "DB_PASSWORD is now available as an environment variable"
      - # Your application code can now access DB_PASSWORD
Notes
  • Grant the CodeBuild service role secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the secret ARN only.
  • Do not echo sensitive variables to logs; use them directly in process environment.
  • Use KMS and audit access to the secret retrieval calls.
Example scenario

In a Node.js integration test stage, the test harness reads DB_PASSWORD from process.env. The CodeBuild role allowed to retrieve the secret provides a short-lived, auditable access path without embedding the password in source.

Common-mistake
Leaving broad '*' permissions on secrets or using a single long-lived token across projects.
Key Takeaway

Map each secret ARN to the minimum set of build projects and never reveal secret values in build logs.

screens.title: Secure build environments and least privilege
screens.narratorSegment: Securing the build environment reduces the blast radius if a build is compromised. Start by using ephemeral build workers so each build runs in a fresh container or VM that is discarded after completion; this prevents persistent backdoors. Next, harden the base image: include only required tooling, remove interactive shells and package managers that are unnecessary, and avoid public images without provenance. For permissions, apply the principle of least privilege to the service role used by CodeBuild. Instead of AdministratorAccess, grant specific actions like s3:GetObject for the source bucket, ecr:PutImage for pushing images, and secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the secrets it needs. Scope resources tightly by ARN whenever possible. Another useful pattern is session-based permissions or short-lived credentials for cross-account access. A common misconception is that a complex policy with many denies is safer; in practice, minimal allow policies bound to exact ARNs are clearer and less error-prone. Concrete example: a build role that only allows GetSecretValue on a single secret ARN and PutImage to a single ECR repository prevents lateral access to other resources. The key outcome: reduce tools, reduce permissions, and reduce lifetime.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Secure build environments
Process Flow

Harden the build lifecycle

1. Ephemeral workers
Ensure builds run on disposable artifacts that are destroyed after use to avoid persistence.
2. Hardened images
Create custom build images with only required tools and keep them updated and scanned.
3. Minimal IAM roles
Grant only the actions and resource ARNs that the build requires.
Example policy focus
Allow ecr:PutImage for arn:aws:ecr:REGION:ACCOUNT:repository/my-app-repo and secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for arn:aws:secretsmanager:REGION:ACCOUNT:secret:my-app/db-api-key. Avoid wildcard actions that allow access to all secrets or all repositories.
Common-mistake
Granting AdministratorAccess or overly broad actions to simplify setup. This creates large attack surfaces when builds are compromised.
Key Takeaway

Scope build permissions and shrink the runtime environment to reduce possible exploitation paths.

screens.title: Container image security and ECR scanning
screens.narratorSegment: When your pipeline builds container images, those images carry OS packages, language libraries, and any tooling in the image. Image scanning helps you detect known vulnerabilities in those components before deployment. Amazon ECR supports integrated image scanning and can be enhanced with Amazon Inspector for deeper checks. The typical architecture is: CodeBuild builds and tags an image, pushes it to an ECR repository where an image scan runs automatically, and the pipeline reads the scan findings before promoting the image to production. You can configure a pipeline stage to fail or block promotion if critical vulnerabilities are found. A practical mistake is assuming a successful build equals a secure artifact; builds can succeed while dependencies contain known CVEs. For example, a Node image using an outdated package could pass tests but have a high-severity CVE; ECR scanning surfaces this so you can update the base image or patch packages. The principle is to treat artifacts as first-class security objects and to build gating logic into promotion steps so unsafe images never reach production. Container image security and ECR scanning means enable ecr image scanning and use scan results as a policy gate to prevent deploying images with critical vulnerabilities.. In practical terms, scan images upon push and gate promotions based on scan results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Container image security
Architecture

Image build and scan pipeline

1. Build
CodeBuild creates the Docker image and tags it.
2. Push
Image is pushed to an ECR repository with scanning enabled.
3. Scan & Gate
ECR runs a scan and the pipeline checks results before promotion.
Example
If the scan reports a critical vulnerability in an OS package, configure the pipeline to fail the promotion stage and notify the team to rebuild with a patched base image.
Operational notes
  • Enable ECR image scanning on push.
  • Automate gating: fail promotions on critical/high CVEs.
  • Use Inspector-enhanced scanning for deeper coverage if available.
Misconception
Relying solely on runtime WAF or host protections; scanning during build prevents deploying vulnerable artifacts in the first place.

screens.title: Automated security testing: SAST, DAST, and SCA
screens.narratorSegment: Automated security testing comprises distinct tools that find different classes of problems. SAST examines source code, bytecode, or binaries without executing them and finds code-level issues like S Q L injection patterns or insecure cryptography use. SCA, or Software Composition Analysis, scans dependency manifests to identify known vulnerable libraries and versions. DAST runs against a running application to identify runtime weaknesses, such as authentication bypass or injection vulnerabilities that only appear during execution. The pipeline best practice is to run SAST and SCA early in the build stage to fail fast on developer-introduced issues and vulnerable dependencies. DAST runs later after deployment to a staging or pre-production environment where the application can be exercised. A common mistake is treating a single tool as sufficient; SAST will not find runtime misconfiguration that DAST would discover, and DAST cannot see source patterns that SAST can. For a concrete example, run Bandit for Python during build to capture common insecure patterns, and run OWASP ZAP in a staging stage to simulate attacks against the running app. The takeaway: integrate all three categories at appropriate pipeline stages and enforce policies for critical findings.

narration.text: Automated security testing comprises distinct tools that find different classes of problems. SAST examines source code, bytecode, or binaries without executing them and finds code-level issues like S Q L injection patterns or insecure cryptography use. SCA, or Software Composition Analysis, scans dependency manifests to identify known vulnerable libraries and versions. DAST runs against a running application to identify runtime weaknesses, such as authentication bypass or injection vulnerabilities that only appear during execution. The pipeline best practice is to run SAST and SCA early in the build stage to fail fast on developer-introduced issues and vulnerable dependencies. DAST runs later after deployment to a staging or pre-production environment where the application can be exercised. A common mistake is treating a single tool as sufficient; SAST will not find runtime misconfiguration that DAST would discover, and DAST cannot see source patterns that SAST can. For a concrete example, run Bandit for Python during build to capture common insecure patterns, and run OWASP ZAP in a staging stage to simulate attacks against the running app. The takeaway: integrate all three categories at appropriate pipeline stages and enforce policies for critical findings.

keyIdea.title: Testing triad
keyIdea.text: Run SAST and SCA during build, and DAST against staged deployments, because each covers different vulnerability classes.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › SAST, DAST & SCA
Comparison

What each test finds

SAST
Static checks on source and binaries for insecure code patterns.
SCA
Dependency scanning for known vulnerabilities in libraries.
DAST
Runtime testing against a running app to find behavior-based issues.
Pipeline placement
  • Run SAST and SCA early in build to fail fast.
  • Run DAST in staging after deployment before production promotion.
Example tools
SAST: Bandit or CodeGuru Security. SCA: Snyk or Dependency-Check. DAST: OWASP ZAP or commercial scanners. Integrate them as steps that output machine-readable reports for gating logic.
Misconception
Assuming one category of tool replaces others. Each addresses different vulnerability classes and should be used together.
Key Takeaway

Combine SAST, SCA, and DAST at the right pipeline stages to detect different classes of vulnerabilities effectively.

screens.title: Common mistakes and mitigations
screens.narratorSegment: Teams repeatedly make a small set of mistakes that create large risks. First, granting overly broad IAM permissions to CI roles is common because it’s quick to set up. The fix is to enumerate only the actions and ARNs the build needs: source retrieval, secret get on explicit ARNs, and push rights to a specific ECR repository. Second, printing secrets in build logs for debugging is frequent but extremely dangerous; implement log hygiene policies and design tests that avoid secret echoes. Third, using public or unproven base images without scanning introduces supply chain risk. Always scan custom images and pick maintained base images. Fourth, ignoring scan results is a human failure mode: pipeline teams must decide whether critical findings should block promotion and automate the enforcement of that policy. Fifth, failing to rotate credentials makes exposure long-lived; enforce rotation where possible, especially for database credentials. For mitigation, adopt least privilege, central secrets, scan artifacts early, and automate gating on critical failures. A quick exercise: review your CodeBuild role and remove any wildcard resource or action. The core insight: policies and processes are as important as tools.

keyIdea.text: Eliminate wildcards in IAM policies, never print secrets, scan and update base images, rotate credentials, and automate gating on critical findings.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Common mistakes

Frequent errors

  • Broad IAM permissions on CodeBuild/CodePipeline roles
  • Echoing secrets into build logs for debugging
  • Using unscanned public base images
  • Ignoring ECR/SAST/SCA scan results
  • Not rotating credentials

Mitigations

Policy hardening
Replace wildcard policies with least-privilege allow lists scoped to ARNs.
Log hygiene
Prevent secrets from being printed; redact or avoid including them in diagnostic outputs.
Automated gating
Fail pipeline promotions when critical scan results are present.
Pro tip

Treat scan alerts as part of your backlog triage and set a policy for acceptable risk levels so teams know when to pause promotions.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: Secrets + ECR scanning in CodeBuild
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on scenario guides you through creating a secret, enabling ECR scanning, and configuring a CodeBuild project to retrieve the secret and push a Docker image. Begin by creating a Secrets Manager secret named my-app/db-api-key with a dummy JSON payload and restrict its resource policy so only the specific CodeBuild role and your application role can retrieve it. Next, enable enhanced scanning for the ECR repository or create a new repository with scanning on push. Then create a CodeBuild project with a service role that has scoped permissions: secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the secret ARN, ecr:PutImage and related image permissions only for the target repository, and minimal source access. In buildspec, reference the secret ARN under env -> secrets-manager and build a simple Docker image, tag it, and push to ECR. After the build completes, check the ECR console for scan results and ensure any critical findings cause an alert or a pipeline fail. A safety note: never echo the secret in build commands; use environment variables directly inside the application. This lab reinforces the full flow from secret creation to scanned artifact promotion.

keyIdea.title: Lab outcome
keyIdea.text: Practice creating a secret, scoping role permissions, building and pushing a Docker image, and verifying ECR scanning results without exposing secrets.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Hands-on activity
Lab Steps
  1. Create Secrets Manager secret named my-app/db-api-key with a dummy value.
  2. Enable ECR image scanning or create a repository with scanning enabled.
  3. Create a CodeBuild project and role with scoped secretsmanager:GetSecretValue and ecr permissions for the repo only.
  4. Update buildspec to reference the secret ARN under env -> secrets-manager, then build, tag, and push the image.
  5. Verify build success and inspect ECR scan results. Configure the pipeline to fail on critical findings.
# Simplified buildspec snippet for lab
version: 0.2
env:
  secrets-manager:
    DB_API_KEY: "arn:aws:secretsmanager:REGION:ACCOUNT_ID:secret:my-app/db-api-key-xxxxxx"
phases:
  pre_build:
    commands:
      - echo "Logging in to Amazon ECR..."
  build:
    commands:
      - docker build -t my-app-image .
      - docker tag my-app-image:latest $AWS_ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.$AWS_DEFAULT_REGION.amazonaws.com/my-app-repo:latest
  post_build:
    commands:
      - docker push $AWS_ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.$AWS_DEFAULT_REGION.amazonaws.com/my-app-repo:latest
Safety notes
  • Do not echo secrets or write them to logs or artifacts.
  • Scope role permissions to the minimal ARNs required.
  • Review ECR scan outputs and treat critical findings as blockers.
Key Takeaway

This lab demonstrates end-to-end secure retrieval of a secret during build and verifying image security before deployment.

screens.title: Pipeline security timeline: shift-left to shift-right
screens.narratorSegment: Security must be distributed across the pipeline timeline. At commit time, enforce pre-commit hooks and SAST checks to prevent obvious issues from entering source control. During build, run SAST and SCA to detect insecure code and vulnerable dependencies. Also in build, resolve secrets at runtime and avoid embedding them in artifacts. After build, push container images to ECR and run automatic image scanning. In the staging deployment stage, run DAST and integration tests to simulate attacks and verify runtime behavior. Finally, before production promotion, evaluate all scan and test results and apply gating logic that prevents images or releases with critical findings from going forward. A common misconception is that security is only a pre-deployment concern; in reality, runtime and post-deployment monitoring are equally essential to catch issues that surface under load or configuration changes. For example, a library vulnerability discovered after deployment should trigger a scheduled rebuild and redeploy with a patched dependency. The timeline approach ensures security is continuous, not a single checkpoint. Pipeline security timeline: shift-left to shift-right means run security checks early (sast/sca), at artifact time (image scans), and later (dast/runtime) so issues are caught at the most effective stage.. In practical terms, map security activities across pipeline stages from commit to production. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Pipeline security timeline
Timeline

From commit to production: security milestones

Commit
Pre-commit hooks, linters, and SAST PR checks.
Build
SAST, SCA, secret retrieval, and unit tests.
Artifact
Push to registry and run ECR image scanning.
Staging
Deploy and run DAST and integration tests.
Production
Final promotion, monitoring, and incident response.
Why staged checks work

Each stage catches different issues at the most cost-effective time: fix code early, patch images before deploy, simulate attacks in staging.

Misconception

Delaying all security to production monitoring assumes prevention failed; staged checks prevent many problems from ever reaching production.

screens.title: Supply chain hygiene and third-party risks
screens.narratorSegment: Supply chain risk arises from third-party components and tools the pipeline depends on: base container images, build plugins, external dependencies, and even CI service integrations. These components can introduce vulnerabilities or malicious code if not vetted. Start by pinning base image versions, choosing images from trusted providers, and scanning them regularly. Audit third-party plugins and tools for maintenance and security posture, and prefer minimal tooling in build images. Maintain an inventory of dependencies and use SCA tools to detect newly discovered CVEs. When using third-party build agents or community-contributed images, assume they may be compromised and limit their permissions accordingly. A practical mitigation is to rebuild third-party images in a controlled environment under your organization’s account, scan the result, and store it in a private registry. Regularly update and replace base images, and automate rebuilds when a critical CVE is announced. The core idea: treat all pipeline components as part of the attack surface and reduce trust where possible. Supply chain hygiene and third-party risks means audit and control third-party base images, plugins, and dependencies; prefer organization-built and scanned artifacts where possible.. In practical terms, audit base images, plugins, and third-party tools used by the pipeline. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Supply chain hygiene

Attack surface: third-party components

Base images, libraries, plugins, and CI tools expand your pipeline's trust boundaries. Vet and control these components.

Inventory
Track base images and dependencies used in your builds and container images.
Rebuild and scan
Rebuild third-party images under your account and scan before trusting them.
Pin and update
Pin versions, track CVE feeds, and trigger rebuilds when critical issues arrive.

Practical steps

  • Use SCA to detect vulnerable dependencies.
  • Scan base images and store trusted snapshots in a private registry.
  • Limit plugin permissions and audit their usage.
Misconception
Assuming widely used open-source images are safe by default; they still require scanning and provenance validation.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to turn a CI/CD pipeline from a potential attack path into a security gate. We will focus on concrete, AWS-native controls: secret management with Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, secure and ephemeral build environments in CodeBuild, container image scanning in ECR, and automated security testing such as SAST, DAST, and SCA. I will show why hardcoding credentials is unsafe, how to grant minimal permissions to build roles, and how to enforce image scan gates before promotion to production. You will also see a practical lab scenario where a Node. js app retrieves a secret during build and then pushes a scanned image to ECR. Notice the pattern: store secrets centrally, grant the pipeline only required access, scan artifacts early, and treat pipeline tooling and base images as part of your attack surface. By the end you will understand the trade-offs between Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, concrete buildspec usage to retrieve secrets, and common mistakes to avoid. Think about one pipeline you manage now and how these steps could reduce supply chain risk.

These objectives map to practical skills you need to secure a CI/CD pipeline on AWS. You will learn to integrate secret stores so credentials are never hardcoded, and to pick the right store for rotation or simple configuration. You will set up static and dynamic testing so vulnerabilities are detected early and later when an app runs. You will configure CodeBuild and ECR to run in hardened, ephemeral environments and scan container images before promotion. Finally, you'll apply least-privilege principles to IAM roles used by pipeline components, limiting what the build process can access. Each objective focuses on both what to configure and why it prevents common supply-chain and deployment risks. For example, instead of embedding an A P I key in source, you will grant CodeBuild short-term access to Secrets Manager and retrieve the value at runtime. Together these skills reduce exposure, enforce policy gates, and make your pipeline auditable. Consider which objective applies first to your pipeline and why it will reduce risk.

This page unpacks how the objectives map to specific risk reductions. Using a centralized secret store prevents credentials from leaking in source control or build logs. Ephemeral CodeBuild workers and hardened build images reduce persistent attack surfaces and limit lateral movement if a build is compromised. Running SAST during build helps catch coding errors before they become deployed flaws, while DAST in staging finds configuration or runtime issues that static analysis cannot. Image scanning catches known vulnerabilities in OS packages or libraries before an image reaches production. Finally, applying least privilege to CI roles stops a compromised build from accessing unrelated resources. Each objective contributes to a layered defense: confidentiality for secrets, integrity for artifacts by scanning and testing, and limited blast radius through IAM scoping. As you progress, ask whether your pipeline fails builds on critical findings or simply logs them; enforcing gates is the difference between detection and prevention.

A CI/CD pipeline automates code movement from source control to production, and that automation makes it powerful but also a high-value target. When we talk about pipeline security, we mean protecting the secrets the pipeline needs, the build and test environments it runs in, the artifacts it produces, and the permissions the pipeline holds. A simple threat model includes credential theft from source or logs, compromised build agents that exfiltrate artifacts, unauthorized promotions to production, and supply-chain insertion of malicious code via third-party dependencies or base images. Defenses map to these threats: secrets must be centralized and rotated so credentials are never committed; build agents should be ephemeral and hardened; artifacts should be scanned for known vulnerabilities, and IAM roles must be tightened with least privilege. A common misconception is that running pipelines in private networks alone is sufficient. Network controls help, but they do not stop leaked secrets or an overprivileged role from acting. For a concrete example, consider an attacker obtaining a long-lived token embedded in a repository — that token can be used to trigger builds and push malicious images. The takeaway: treat the pipeline as code and infrastructure that requires the same security rigor as production systems. How would you prioritize these defenses for your environment?

Secrets are sensitive values required at build or runtime: database passwords, A P I keys, and tokens. Centralized secret management prevents developers from embedding those values in code or configuration files where they can leak. AWS provides two primary services for this purpose: Secrets Manager and Systems Manager Parameter Store. Secrets Manager is designed for credentials and supports automatic rotation for services like databases. It is suited to secrets that require periodic rotation or broad auditing. Parameter Store also supports secure strings and is suitable for configuration values and non-rotating secrets; it is often used for environment-specific parameters or feature flags. The practical difference comes down to rotation features and operational patterns. A common misconception is that Parameter Store is insecure; when used with SecureString and proper KMS keys it is secure, but it lacks Secrets Manager’s built-in rotation workflow. For a concrete example, store a DB password in Secrets Manager and grant CodeBuild’s service role permission to retrieve that secret during build, rather than checking it into source. The key takeaway is to never hardcode secrets: centralize, grant narrowly, and enable rotation when possible.

Choosing between Secrets Manager and Parameter Store depends on your operational needs. Secrets Manager is purpose-built for credentials: it supports built-in rotation with Lambda rotation functions, fine-grained resource policies, and auditing of secret retrieval. Use it when secrets require regular rotation or you need lifecycle automation. Parameter Store, with SecureString, is well suited to configuration, non-rotating secrets, and feature flags, and it can be simpler and lower cost for many parameters. A practical scenario: use Secrets Manager for your database password that should be rotated every 30 days, and use Parameter Store for an environment toggle or a service endpoint URL that rarely changes. A common mistake is mirroring all secrets into a single store without considering rotation risk — rotation workflows should be applied where credentials are used by many services. In pipelines, both services can be retrieved by CodeBuild using env-level secret references. The most important rule is to grant only the required get permissions to your builds and to avoid printing secrets in logs. A short test you can run: ensure secrets are never visible in build logs even when an error occurs.

This screen walks through a typical CodeBuild integration where a secret stored in Secrets Manager is made available to the build as an environment variable. The important idea is that the buildspec references the secret by ARN under the env -> secrets-manager section, and CodeBuild’s service role must be permitted to call GetSecretValue for that secret ARN. The build then uses the environment variable without printing it to logs. A common pitfall is echoing the secret during debugging; never print secrets to stdout. Here is a minimal buildspec pattern: define the secret mapping so CodeBuild resolves the value at runtime, then use it in commands. Remember to scope the service role policy to only that secret and to deny broad wildcard secrets. In practice, you would also ensure the CodeBuild project uses an ephemeral image, and that any custom image is hardened and scanned. The takeaway: runtime secret injection via Secrets Manager eliminates committed credentials, but role permissions and log hygiene must be enforced to keep it safe. Integrating secrets into CodeBuild means reference secrets by arn in buildspec.yml and grant codebuild getsecretvalue only for those arns; never echo secrets in logs.. In practical terms, using buildspec.yml to retrieve secrets manager values securely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Securing the build environment reduces the blast radius if a build is compromised. Start by using ephemeral build workers so each build runs in a fresh container or VM that is discarded after completion; this prevents persistent backdoors. Next, harden the base image: include only required tooling, remove interactive shells and package managers that are unnecessary, and avoid public images without provenance. For permissions, apply the principle of least privilege to the service role used by CodeBuild. Instead of AdministratorAccess, grant specific actions like s3:GetObject for the source bucket, ecr:PutImage for pushing images, and secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the secrets it needs. Scope resources tightly by ARN whenever possible. Another useful pattern is session-based permissions or short-lived credentials for cross-account access. A common misconception is that a complex policy with many denies is safer; in practice, minimal allow policies bound to exact ARNs are clearer and less error-prone. Concrete example: a build role that only allows GetSecretValue on a single secret ARN and PutImage to a single ECR repository prevents lateral access to other resources. The key outcome: reduce tools, reduce permissions, and reduce lifetime.

When your pipeline builds container images, those images carry OS packages, language libraries, and any tooling in the image. Image scanning helps you detect known vulnerabilities in those components before deployment. Amazon ECR supports integrated image scanning and can be enhanced with Amazon Inspector for deeper checks. The typical architecture is: CodeBuild builds and tags an image, pushes it to an ECR repository where an image scan runs automatically, and the pipeline reads the scan findings before promoting the image to production. You can configure a pipeline stage to fail or block promotion if critical vulnerabilities are found. A practical mistake is assuming a successful build equals a secure artifact; builds can succeed while dependencies contain known CVEs. For example, a Node image using an outdated package could pass tests but have a high-severity CVE; ECR scanning surfaces this so you can update the base image or patch packages. The principle is to treat artifacts as first-class security objects and to build gating logic into promotion steps so unsafe images never reach production. Container image security and ECR scanning means enable ecr image scanning and use scan results as a policy gate to prevent deploying images with critical vulnerabilities.. In practical terms, scan images upon push and gate promotions based on scan results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Automated security testing comprises distinct tools that find different classes of problems. SAST examines source code, bytecode, or binaries without executing them and finds code-level issues like S Q L injection patterns or insecure cryptography use. SCA, or Software Composition Analysis, scans dependency manifests to identify known vulnerable libraries and versions. DAST runs against a running application to identify runtime weaknesses, such as authentication bypass or injection vulnerabilities that only appear during execution. The pipeline best practice is to run SAST and SCA early in the build stage to fail fast on developer-introduced issues and vulnerable dependencies. DAST runs later after deployment to a staging or pre-production environment where the application can be exercised. A common mistake is treating a single tool as sufficient; SAST will not find runtime misconfiguration that DAST would discover, and DAST cannot see source patterns that SAST can. For a concrete example, run Bandit for Python during build to capture common insecure patterns, and run OWASP ZAP in a staging stage to simulate attacks against the running app. The takeaway: integrate all three categories at appropriate pipeline stages and enforce policies for critical findings.

Teams repeatedly make a small set of mistakes that create large risks. First, granting overly broad IAM permissions to CI roles is common because it’s quick to set up. The fix is to enumerate only the actions and ARNs the build needs: source retrieval, secret get on explicit ARNs, and push rights to a specific ECR repository. Second, printing secrets in build logs for debugging is frequent but extremely dangerous; implement log hygiene policies and design tests that avoid secret echoes. Third, using public or unproven base images without scanning introduces supply chain risk. Always scan custom images and pick maintained base images. Fourth, ignoring scan results is a human failure mode: pipeline teams must decide whether critical findings should block promotion and automate the enforcement of that policy. Fifth, failing to rotate credentials makes exposure long-lived; enforce rotation where possible, especially for database credentials. For mitigation, adopt least privilege, central secrets, scan artifacts early, and automate gating on critical failures. A quick exercise: review your CodeBuild role and remove any wildcard resource or action. The core insight: policies and processes are as important as tools.

This hands-on scenario guides you through creating a secret, enabling ECR scanning, and configuring a CodeBuild project to retrieve the secret and push a Docker image. Begin by creating a Secrets Manager secret named my-app/db-api-key with a dummy JSON payload and restrict its resource policy so only the specific CodeBuild role and your application role can retrieve it. Next, enable enhanced scanning for the ECR repository or create a new repository with scanning on push. Then create a CodeBuild project with a service role that has scoped permissions: secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the secret ARN, ecr:PutImage and related image permissions only for the target repository, and minimal source access. In buildspec, reference the secret ARN under env -> secrets-manager and build a simple Docker image, tag it, and push to ECR. After the build completes, check the ECR console for scan results and ensure any critical findings cause an alert or a pipeline fail. A safety note: never echo the secret in build commands; use environment variables directly inside the application. This lab reinforces the full flow from secret creation to scanned artifact promotion.

Security must be distributed across the pipeline timeline. At commit time, enforce pre-commit hooks and SAST checks to prevent obvious issues from entering source control. During build, run SAST and SCA to detect insecure code and vulnerable dependencies. Also in build, resolve secrets at runtime and avoid embedding them in artifacts. After build, push container images to ECR and run automatic image scanning. In the staging deployment stage, run DAST and integration tests to simulate attacks and verify runtime behavior. Finally, before production promotion, evaluate all scan and test results and apply gating logic that prevents images or releases with critical findings from going forward. A common misconception is that security is only a pre-deployment concern; in reality, runtime and post-deployment monitoring are equally essential to catch issues that surface under load or configuration changes. For example, a library vulnerability discovered after deployment should trigger a scheduled rebuild and redeploy with a patched dependency. The timeline approach ensures security is continuous, not a single checkpoint. Pipeline security timeline: shift-left to shift-right means run security checks early (sast/sca), at artifact time (image scans), and later (dast/runtime) so issues are caught at the most effective stage.. In practical terms, map security activities across pipeline stages from commit to production. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Supply chain risk arises from third-party components and tools the pipeline depends on: base container images, build plugins, external dependencies, and even CI service integrations. These components can introduce vulnerabilities or malicious code if not vetted. Start by pinning base image versions, choosing images from trusted providers, and scanning them regularly. Audit third-party plugins and tools for maintenance and security posture, and prefer minimal tooling in build images. Maintain an inventory of dependencies and use SCA tools to detect newly discovered CVEs. When using third-party build agents or community-contributed images, assume they may be compromised and limit their permissions accordingly. A practical mitigation is to rebuild third-party images in a controlled environment under your organization’s account, scan the result, and store it in a private registry. Regularly update and replace base images, and automate rebuilds when a critical CVE is announced. The core idea: treat all pipeline components as part of the attack surface and reduce trust where possible. Supply chain hygiene and third-party risks means audit and control third-party base images, plugins, and dependencies; prefer organization-built and scanned artifacts where possible.. Here are three essential concepts to take away. First, secret management: store secrets in Secrets Manager or Parameter Store SecureString and retrieve them in builds rather than hardcoding. Second, least privilege for CI roles: scope IAM policies to specific actions and ARNs to limit what a compromised build can do. Third, image scanning and automated tests: run SAST/SCA during build and ECR image scans on push, plus DAST in staging, and make scan results enforceable gates. These three together secure credentials, reduce artifact risk, and limit blast radius. Keep them in mind as a short checklist you can apply immediately. Second, audit and rebuild third-party base images under your account, then scan them before use.
